title: In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to convert bitumen underground into oil that can enter a specified receiving pipeline without added diluent or surface upgrading. Success would require sustained product quality across a commercial production pattern—a coordinated arrangement of injection and production wells—rather than a brief improvement in a laboratory sample. The defining advance is sufficient molecular conversion inside the reservoir, beyond simply heating bitumen until it flows.

Toe-to-heel air injection, or THAI, provides one route toward this goal. Underground combustion supplies heat that mobilizes and thermally cracks heavy oil or bitumen while the oil travels a short distance to a horizontal production well. CAPRI adds a catalyst bed around that producer so that partially upgraded oil undergoes further reactions before entering the well. This configuration motivates the idea of using part of the reservoir as a chemical reactor, but does not itself establish sustained production of pipeline-compliant oil.

Scope synthesis: THAI-CAPRI is a documented approach to the broader target, not a required architecture for every possible solution. The target is an undiluted product meeting the applicable receiving-pipeline requirements, produced without a surface upgrader over a commercially meaningful scale and duration. Pipeline acceptance does not necessarily require the product to become light crude.

significance.text: If successful, sufficient conversion underground could remove the need for transport diluent and surface upgrading to obtain the specified product from the production patterns where the process worked. The direct consequence would be a change in the quality and transportability of the liquid leaving the reservoir. The documented THAI-CAPRI research pursues easier oil transport and reduced surface upgrading, providing a technical basis for this conditional impact.

Conditional downstream synthesis: avoiding those requirements could simplify parts of the production and transport system and change where processing equipment and investment are needed. The benefit would depend on the resources and equipment required underground, including heat, air, hydrogen where used, and catalyst management. Pipeline acceptance alone establishes neither universal refinery compatibility nor profitability. It also does not establish lower emissions; energy use, combustion, hydrogen supply and other process burdens would need separate assessment. No percentage emissions reduction is supported here.

The underground-reactor analogy captures the relocation of molecular conversion into the formation. It should not imply that the reservoir offers the same control, accessibility or maintenance options as a surface processing plant. In THAI-CAPRI, the documented difficulty of maintaining catalyst effectiveness is central to whether the analogy can become a practical production capability.

The concept belongs to the broader research ambition of manipulating petroleum molecules in situ. A Journal of Petroleum Technology article dated December 31, 2015 lists this ambition among the SPE Research and Development Committee's grand challenges. That historical context establishes a research goal, not a successful field demonstration or a quantified impact.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is a reservoir reaction zone that repeatedly converts contacted extra-heavy oil into an undiluted, pipeline-acceptable product throughout a commercial pattern and a commercially meaningful operating period. Existing evidence of thermal upgrading, additional catalytic conversion and short experimental runs addresses parts of that requirement. It does not, in the supplied record, establish the complete sustained capability.

For catalytic approaches, maintaining access to active catalyst surfaces is a concrete obstacle. Coke can block catalyst pores and reduce effectiveness. Muhammad Rabiu Ado's paper identifies this as a major limitation and emphasizes the need to understand how to maximize catalyst life before field deployment. Its literature discussion reports different upgrading gains across experiments, so the barrier cannot accurately be reduced to a universal rule that every catalyst adds only a few API degrees before failing.

The relationship between catalytic contact, temperature and useful operating life also remains important. CAPRI requires thermally altered oil to reach and contact the catalyst bed. Ado's study investigates catalyst-packing porosity through experimental-scale numerical simulations, while assuming an externally heated catalyst layer of at least 400 °C and supplying hydrogen with air. These conditions leave open how comparable reaction conditions and sustained conversion would be established and maintained in a commercial reservoir.

Engineering synthesis: scale-up must connect reaction performance to the entire produced stream. A process would need adequate contact between oil and the reactive zone, sufficient heat and reactant delivery, and manageable loss of activity without unacceptable disruption to production. It must maintain all specified pipeline-acceptance properties as operating conditions and the contacted reservoir volume change. A favorable density or viscosity measurement alone cannot resolve those combined requirements.

current_state.text: Ado's original numerical-simulation paper was published online in October 2021 and issued in 2022. Its literature discussion reports a single Whitesands THAI-CAPRI pilot test in 2008. That test reportedly achieved additional upgrading beyond THAI's thermal effect, but the increment was judged insufficient to continue the catalytic add-on. This is a historical pilot outcome reported by the paper; it does not independently establish every subsequent deployment decision.

The supplied research attributes a roughly five-year Whitesands THAI operating period, from 2006 to 2011, and a field upgrading gain of about 4–5 API degrees to a 2017 experimental paper. However, no artifact of that paper was retained for the supplied review, so those figures remain attributed but unverified in this record. This limitation does not demonstrate that the figures are false. The reported duration concerns the broader THAI pilot and should not be treated as five years of sustained CAPRI operation.

Laboratory outcomes summarized by Ado vary. One cited experiment reported a maximum additional upgrading gain of 3 API degrees at an optimum temperature of 420 °C, with catalyst life of roughly 3.25 days. Another cited study reported an additional 4–7 API degrees beyond a 10-degree gain from thermal upgrading. These are literature results as summarized in Ado's paper, rather than independently verified original experiments in the supplied review. They demonstrate why upgrading magnitude and durability must be assessed together, while contradicting a blanket few-degree ceiling for all catalysts.

Ado's own study uses experimental-scale numerical simulations lasting 320 minutes. It supplies hydrogen with air and treats the catalyst layer as externally heated to at least 400 °C during catalytic reactions. Its modeled results therefore do not demonstrate sustained commercial field performance. These assumptions also do not, by themselves, establish that commercial operation is fundamentally infeasible. The supplied review evaluated the article's text and PDF; figure images were not inspected.

The Alberta Energy Regulator reserves page updated in September 2026 describes in-situ bitumen production using steam-assisted gravity drainage and cyclic steam stimulation. Its reserve estimates are effective December 31, 2023, rather than September 2026. The retained material available to the review omitted an image or table, limiting completeness. The page supports the stated Alberta production methods, but reserve classification is not an inventory of every upgrading technology and cannot establish worldwide technological absence.

The complete capability's worldwide status as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved by the supplied evidence. Ado's introduction broadly describes combustion processes as producing transportable light oils, but the reviewed passages do not identify a receiving-pipeline specification or document sustained commercial compliance with every requirement. That broad description neither verifies this entry's full target nor supports an unqualified assertion that no qualifying operation exists. The supplied review contains no freshness-search record that would settle present-day deployment.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: operate one commercial-scale production pattern with no added diluent and no surface upgrading, delivering oil that meets every acceptance requirement of a named receiving pipeline under the applicable rules. Declare the operating period in advance, with months of sustained production as an initial proposed threshold. Specify pattern dimensions, production rate, sampling conditions, allowable interruptions and how every acceptance requirement will be measured.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained pipeline-compliant pattern production uses no diluent or surface upgrading

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability evidence: use a measurable end-of-test assessment to show that the reactive zone or catalyst remains effective, supported by production and product-quality records across the declared period. The assessment should distinguish ongoing conversion from a short initial improvement or changes in the oil entering the process. A catalyst-based design should define what counts as continuing activity and report replacement, regeneration or other interventions.
completion_criteria.label: End-of-test assessment confirms continued reactive zone or catalyst effectiveness

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independently verify representative product measurements and repeat sustained performance in another operating interval or pattern, documenting reservoir conditions and process inputs. The result should establish the conditions under which the demonstrated performance can be reproduced. Finite demonstrations establish a tested range of reservoirs and operating conditions, not literal universality across bitumen deposits.
completion_criteria.label: Independent verification and sustained replication establish reproducible conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundaries: a few API degrees of improvement or a microreactor result alone would not satisfy the target. A viscosity reduction would qualify only if the produced oil also met every named pipeline requirement; continued classification as heavy oil would not automatically disqualify it. A months-long demonstration would establish sustained field performance over that interval, while full commercial lifetime, profitability, refinery suitability and environmental performance would remain separate questions.
completion_criteria.label: Claims limit sustained field performance to the demonstrated interval

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: PET-09, Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature, concerns mobilization without relying on a hot reservoir to make the bitumen flow. PET-11 concerns sufficient conversion of contacted bitumen to produce pipeline-acceptable oil and may use a hot reaction front. Improved mobility can assist production without achieving PET-11's product-quality target; achieving PET-11 through heating would not establish PET-09.

Roster-based distinction: PET-04, Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen, also places chemical conversion underground, but begins with kerogen that has not yet become oil. PET-11 begins with bitumen and targets the quality of the produced crude. Shared heating or reaction-control methods would not make the feedstocks or demonstration requirements interchangeable.

Roster-based distinction: PET-06, Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground, targets hydrogen as the sold product and retention of other products in the formation. PET-11 targets a produced liquid crude stream. Both fit the broad ambition of in-situ molecular manipulation, and one future process might address aspects of both, but success at producing hydrogen would not demonstrate pipeline-compliant crude production.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-01, Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow, and PET-08, Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume, could help design or assess fluid contact and production patterns. PET-02 and PET-05 focus on recovery performance, whereas PET-11 focuses on the quality of the recovered liquid. These are possible enabling relationships, not requirements to merge the entries. The supplied roster provides titles rather than full neighboring records, so precise scope boundaries beyond the supplied descriptions remain provisional.

change_log.change: Preserved PET-11's identity while defining success as sustained, undiluted receiving-pipeline compliance without surface upgrading.
change_log.reason: The central innovation is coherent; uncertainty about supporting assertions does not justify removing or relabeling the concept.

change_log.change: Separated the THAI thermal mechanism from CAPRI's additional catalytic contact and distinguished the broader THAI pilot from the reported 2008 CAPRI test.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports these distinct stages and histories, but does not support treating the broader pilot duration as sustained catalytic operation.

change_log.change: Retained the attributed 2006–2011 operating period and 4–5 API-degree field gain with explicit verification limits.
change_log.reason: The cited 2017 source was not captured for review. Missing evidence warrants qualification rather than rejection of the figures.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal few-degree laboratory limit with specific, varied experimental results and a separate durability problem.
change_log.reason: Ado's literature discussion reports both a short-lived 3-degree result and larger additional gains in another experiment.

change_log.change: Identified Ado's source as an original simulation paper published online in 2021 and issued in 2022, and included its run duration and modeling assumptions.
change_log.reason: Its literature discussion and modeled results carry different evidentiary weight; neither establishes sustained commercial operation.

change_log.change: Removed categorical worldwide non-deployment and broadly unfavorable feasibility conclusions.
change_log.reason: Historical difficulties, an incomplete contemporary search record and Alberta reserve categories do not establish worldwide absence or fundamental infeasibility.

change_log.change: Qualified the AER evidence with the December 31, 2023 reserve date and the review's missing image or table.
change_log.reason: The September 2026 page update does not make the reserve estimates contemporaneous or turn the page into a comprehensive technology inventory.

change_log.change: Removed the implication that pipeline acceptance means light crude, universal refinery compatibility or established economic and emissions benefits.
change_log.reason: Those consequences require separate evidence and do not follow from meeting a receiving pipeline's requirements.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to specify acceptance measurements, operating conditions, continuing activity, repeatability and limits of inference.
change_log.reason: A field demonstration needs measurable boundaries; proposed months-long thresholds are not established standards or proof of commercial lifetime.

change_log.change: Preserved neighboring concepts as distinct entries and corrected the JPT historical reference to December 31, 2015.
change_log.reason: The supplied roster supports useful conceptual comparisons without independent verification of full neighboring scopes; the reviewed article supplies the corrected date.

unresolved_issues: The 2017 paper's attributed Whitesands duration and 4–5 API-degree field gain remain unverified because no source artifact was supplied for review.
The supplied evidence does not determine whether any operation worldwide had achieved the complete target capability by November 1, 2026.
The broad description of transportable light oils in Ado's introduction is not accompanied in the reviewed passages by a named pipeline specification and sustained commercial compliance record.
The original experimental reports summarized by Ado were not independently verified in the supplied review; their numerical results retain that attribution.

A receiving pipeline, its applicable acceptance requirements, commercial pattern dimensions, production rate, test duration and measurable activity endpoint remain to be selected for an actual demonstration.
Commercial catalyst lifetime, maintenance requirements and the practical provision of heat and reactants remain unresolved at the target scale.
Profitability, refinery suitability and lifecycle emissions cannot be inferred from pipeline compliance and require separate evaluation.
Full neighboring concept records were not supplied, so the related-concept boundaries remain based on the roster and supplied descriptions.

brief.title: Oil made ready for pipelines while still underground
possible: Oil producers could bring bitumen, a very thick form of oil, out of the ground ready for a receiving pipeline. Chemical reactions underground would change the oil itself, removing the need to mix in thinning liquids or process it in a surface plant before transport.
why: For producers, this could simplify the equipment and supplies needed to prepare oil for transport. More of the processing would happen where the oil lies, changing where processing plants and investment are needed.

sources.showed: Meehan described the petroleum industry's research challenges, including changing petroleum molecules underground.
sources.cited_for: Changing oil molecules underground is an established research ambition.
sources.not_established: Identifying a research goal does not demonstrate oil production that meets pipeline requirements.

sources.who: Alberta Energy Regulator and McDaniel and Associates Consultants Ltd.
sources.showed: They evaluated Alberta's oil and gas reserves and resources. The regulator also describes steam-based methods for producing bitumen underground.
sources.quote: The evaluations incorporate effectively 100% of the provincial oil and gas production and were completed using publicly available data.
sources.cited_for: The regulator describes established methods of producing Alberta's bitumen.
sources.not_established: A reserves assessment does not establish sustained underground conversion into oil that meets pipeline requirements.

sources.showed: This is a laboratory investigation of a catalyst-assisted process for producing and chemically changing heavy oil underground.
sources.cited_for: The paper is cited for historical reports of field operation and changes in oil quality at Whitesands.
sources.not_established: Those reports do not establish sustained production without thinning liquids that meets every receiving-pipeline requirement.

sources.showed: Ado's computer simulations found that leaving more space between catalyst particles improved oil quality. Catalysts are materials that help chemical reactions occur.
sources.quote: the larger the catalyst packing porosity, the higher the accessible surface area for the mobilized oil to reach the inner coke-uncoated catalysts and thus the higher the API gravity and quality of the produced oil
sources.cited_for: Simulations connect access to catalyst surfaces with improved oil quality.
sources.not_established: Short simulations with added heat and hydrogen do not establish lasting performance in a commercial reservoir.

shown: Ado reports that a Whitesands field pilot combined underground burning with a catalyst bed around a production well. The catalyst improved oil beyond the effect of heat alone, but the improvement was judged too small to continue the catalyst addition.

Ado's own work used short computer simulations. These showed how catalyst spacing could improve conversion, while assuming added heat and hydrogen. They did not demonstrate sustained commercial production meeting a named pipeline's requirements.
missing: A commercial demonstration still needs to deliver oil meeting every receiving-pipeline requirement without thinning liquids or surface processing.
The underground reaction zone must keep working as production continues, with manageable maintenance and loss of catalyst activity where catalysts are used.
Heat, reactants and contact with the oil must remain sufficient across the whole producing area.
Independent measurements and repeated sustained operation must establish where the process works reliably.

milestones.label: Sustained commercial production meets every pipeline requirement
milestones.explanation: A commercial group of injection and production wells would have to meet a named pipeline's rules for a declared period of months without thinning liquids or surface processing. This would demonstrate the complete capability.

milestones.label: The reaction zone remains effective through the test
milestones.explanation: An end-of-test assessment and production history would have to confirm continuing conversion and document maintenance. This would distinguish lasting activity from an initial improvement or a change in incoming oil.

milestones.label: Independent checks and repeated operation confirm reproducibility
milestones.explanation: Independent product checks and another sustained operating interval or group of wells would have to repeat the result with documented conditions and inputs. This would establish the conditions under which performance is reproducible.

milestones.label: Performance claims stay within the demonstrated limits
milestones.explanation: Claims would have to match the tested duration and all pipeline requirements; thinner oil alone would not qualify. This would keep sustained field performance separate from lifetime, profit, refinery and environmental claims.

uncertain: Whether any operation already meets the complete target remains unresolved.
Commercial catalyst life and the practical supply of heat and reactants remain open questions.
The receiving pipeline, test duration, production scale and measure of continuing reaction activity still need to be defined.
